The Yellowmouth rockfish (Sebastes reedi) attains a maximum total length of 58 centimeters [Li = 58 centimeters], a size commonly observed among older individuals inhabiting the outer continental shelf off British Columbia. Females typically reach the onset of sexual maturation at a total length of approximately 35 centimeters [Lp = approximately 35 centimeters], a threshold that marks the beginning of gonad development and the transition to the reproductively active adult stage. The body mass of a fish at this pubertal milestone has been estimated at around 590 grams [Wwp = around 590 grams], based on established length-weight relationships for this species. In contrast, the ultimate body mass achieved by fully grown adults can be substantially greater, with the heaviest individuals reaching approximately 2.8 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 2.8 kilograms]. This considerable increase in somatic mass between puberty and the asymptotic size reflects the protracted period of post-maturational growth characteristic of many Sebastes species, which continue to add length and weight slowly throughout much of their long lives.

Reproductive output in Yellowmouth rockfish has been studied primarily through estimates derived from closely related congeners, given the logistical challenges of direct observation in this deepwater viviparous species. Under stable thermal conditions typical of its benthic habitat at 5.4 °C [T = 5.4 °C], the maximum annual fecundity of an individual female is approximately 1,100,000 larvae per year [Ri = approximately 1,100,000 larvae per year]. This figure, which integrates both the high fecundity associated with a single parturition event and the interval between successive spawnings, underscores the considerable reproductive potential of this species. The observed rate is consistent with values reported for Sebastes entomelas under comparable thermal regimes, lending support to the hypothesis that reproductive physiology is evolutionarily conserved within this genus. Such a high annual larval production, maintained over the extended spawning season, represents a significant energetic investment for each mature female.

The earliest developmental stages of Yellowmouth rockfish are characterised by a remarkably small initial body mass. At the time of parturition, the weight of each newly extruded larva is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a value that reflects the modest diameter of the yolked oocyte from which it develops. Despite the viviparous mode of reproduction typical of the genus Sebastinae, this larval mass is comparable to that of many oviparous teleosts that produce pelagic eggs in the 0.8 millimeter diameter range. The yolk-sac larva, which is still endotrophic immediately following emergence, must rely entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves to sustain metabolic demands until the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition from this lecithotrophic phase to the active capture of planktonic prey marks a critical bottleneck in early life history, as larval survival hinges on the timely inflation of the swim bladder and the differentiation of the retinal system for prey detection.

Longevity in Yellowmouth rockfish is exceptional, with the maximum recorded lifespan of the species estimated at 99 years [am = 99 years] at the ambient temperature of 5.4 °C [T = 5.4 °C]. This extreme duration of life places Sebastes reedi among the most long-lived teleosts known from the North Pacific Ocean, a group that includes several other rockfish species with lifespans exceeding a century. The physiological mechanisms underlying such pronounced longevity are believed to involve low basal metabolic rates, reduced oxidative damage accumulation, and efficient cellular repair pathways, all of which are favoured in the cold, stable, food-limited environment of the outer continental slope. At this temperature, metabolic demands are low, allowing the species to allocate energy toward somatic maintenance rather than rapid growth or frequent reproduction. This life-history strategy, characterised by slow growth, delayed maturity, and extreme iteroparity, stands in stark contrast to that of short-lived, high-fecundity species occupying warmer, more variable nearshore habitats.

The demersal spawning behaviour of Yellowmouth rockfish occurs over rocky outcrops and boulder fields at depths between 150 and 350 meters, where females release fully developed, free-swimming larvae during the late winter and early spring months. These larvae, measuring only a few millimeters in total length immediately after parturition, ascend into the pelagic zone to begin an extended planktonic phase that may last several months. During this period, the growing juveniles feed on copepods, euphausiids, and other small zooplankton before eventually settling to the seafloor as benthic juveniles. The transition from a pelagic larva to a demersal juvenile, known as larval settlement, coincides with the onset of morphological transformations including fin ray ossification and the development of the characteristic yellow pigmentation around the mouth that gives the species its common name. This protracted settlement window, combined with the species' extreme longevity, suggests that recruitment variability is buffered by the presence of multiple overlapping year classes in the spawning stock.
